content: Statistics New Zealand, also known in Māori as Tatauranga Aotearoa, is the government agency in New Zealand responsible for producing the country’s official statistics. This responsibility is granted under the authority of the Statistics Act of 1975. Prior to 1994, the organisation was referred to as the Department of Statistics. The current Minister of Statistics is the Honorable Clayton Cosgrove. The organisation has a broad range of responsibilities. It oversees the collection, analysis, and dissemination of statistical data, including conducting the national census every five years. Many of the statistics produced are made freely available to the public through its official website. Additionally, Statistics New Zealand is responsible for developing statistical classifications and standards specific to the country. It also engages in ongoing research and development to refine statistical methodologies. Beyond its domestic role, the organisation provides technical assistance to developing nations in the Pacific region, with a particular emphasis on supporting Pacific Island countries. Statistics New Zealand plays a pivotal role in leading and promoting the development of government statistics that form part of New Zealand’s Official Statistics System. This includes coordinating the country’s first integrated programme of Official Social Statistics. The chief executive officer of Statistics New Zealand holds the title of Government Statistician. The individuals who have held this position include: John Darwin (1980–1984) Steve Kuzmicich (1984–1992) Len Cook (1992–1999) Brian Pink (1999–2007) Geoff Bascand (2007–present) In 2005, Statistics New Zealand was ranked as the 18th most desirable employer for graduates in Australasia. This recognition is largely attributed to its graduate Leadership Development Programme (gLDP). The gLDP is designed to cultivate future leadership capabilities within Statistics New Zealand and the broader New Zealand Public Service. The programme provides graduates with opportunities to develop leadership skills through a structured and innovative framework. Participants in the gLDP benefit from social and technical support networks, monthly workshops, peer mentoring, action learning groups, and collaborative team projects. During the first year of the programme, graduates complete three rotational assignments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the organisation. As they progress, they are entrusted with greater responsibilities, including project management roles. Statistics New Zealand is widely recognised as a learning organisation, and the gLDP exemplifies its commitment to professional development. The Statistics New Zealand website specifies that information obtained from the organisation may be freely used, reproduced, or quoted unless otherwise stated. However, in all instances, Statistics New Zealand must be acknowledged as the source of the information.
